title: The opening of the chest
hook: Muslim reports that as a boy his chest was opened by angels and his heart washed

segments.voice: Yesterday, Halimah's thin donkey. Your line was: blessing came with him. Whose arrival did you name, and did you tell them? Day seven hundred eight.

Boys are playing in the open country of the Banu Sa'd. Suddenly they scatter and run, shouting to the boy's foster mother: Muhammad has been killed! The family rushes out and finds him alive, his face pale. Something has happened to him that the other children saw only from a distance. Sahih Muslim keeps the account, from Anas ibn Malik, a companion of the Prophet ﷺ. Today: the opening of the chest.
screen: `BOYS AT PLAY.` → `"MUHAMMAD HAS BEEN KILLED!"` → `ALIVE, AND PALE.`

segments.voice: Here is what Muslim reports. While the boy was playing, Jibril came to him, laid him down, and opened his chest. He took out the heart, and from it drew out a clot, and said: this was the share of Satan in you. Then he washed the heart in a basin of gold, with the water of Zamzam, the well his grandfather found again, and put it back in its place. Anas adds a small detail that brings the whole thing close: he says he used to see the mark of the stitching on the Prophet's chest. Ibn Ishaq tells the same event in Halimah's voice, with two men in white, and says it frightened the family into taking the boy back to his mother in Mecca. So the sources differ on the details, and say so. What does the story mean? Readers take it in different ways. Some take it as a real event that happened to his body. Others stress what it points to: a heart prepared early, cleaned of what pulls toward harm, before anything was asked of it. Some commentators connect it with the opening of surah ninety-four, which Pickthall translates: "Have We not caused thy bosom to dilate." The Arabic there speaks of opening, or expanding, the chest. Notice what the story does not say. It doesn't say the boy did anything to earn it. He was playing. The washing came to him, the way water comes to a dry field. And notice the water: not something exotic, but Zamzam, the well from a few days ago, the water of Hajar's search.
screen: `JIBRIL OPENS THE CHEST.` · `WASHED WITH ZAMZAM IN A GOLD BASIN.` · `ANAS SAW THE STITCHING MARK.` · `A HEART PREPARED EARLY.` · then, large: `HAVE WE NOT CAUSED THY BOSOM TO DILATE.`

segments.voice: The practice: wash your hands and face slowly. If there's water near you, go to it now. If not, do this in your mind, just as slowly. Let cool water run over your hands. Feel the wrists, the palms, the space between the fingers. Then cup the water and bring it to your face. Hold it there for a breath. Muslims wash before prayer in a set order; this is not that, just a slow washing. As the water goes, let one thing you've been carrying go with it. If you pray, you can ask Allah for a clean heart in your own words. The bell holds the time.
The opening of the chest. In Sahih Muslim, Jibril opens the boy's chest, draws out the share of Satan, and washes the heart with Zamzam. Today's word.
screen: `THE OPENING OF THE CHEST — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: a washed heart. Today, each time you wash your hands, let it be slow for one breath, and set down one grudge with the water. Day seven hundred eight.

howItsDone: Muslims know this event as sharh al-sadr, the opening of the chest; it is retold in sirah and hadith study, and some connect it with the opening of surah al-Sharh (94).

fork.setup: you're one of the boys playing with him. a stranger lays him down and opens his chest. what do you do?
options: run to his foster mother shouting.
fork.reveal: Muslim reports the boys ran to his foster mother saying he'd been killed; they found him alive and pale.

original.note: Arabic: the opening, or expanding, of the chest; surah 94 begins with a verb from the same root.

trapdoor: what you thought: a strange story about surgery.
what it means: a heart washed and prepared early, before anything was asked of him.
what a scholar hears: Muslim's report from Anas, with Zamzam and a gold basin; Ibn Ishaq's version differs in detail; some link it to 94:1.

notes: The index hook says 'angels'; Sahih Muslim names Jibril, and Ibn Ishaq tells of two men in white. The script gives both and says the sources differ. Confirm.
Sahih Muslim number (162 in the common numbering) cited from memory; confirm, and confirm that Anas's stitching remark is in the same report.
Pickthall 94:1 ('Have We not caused thy bosom to dilate,') quoted from memory; confirm wording.
'Some take it as a real event... others stress what it points to' describes a range of readings without ranking; a Keeper may want to name which schools or scholars hold which view.
The practice explicitly says it is not wudu, to avoid teaching an incomplete ablution. Confirm that framing.
Anas 'served the Prophet for years in Medina' is stated without a count; confirm.
